title: Poetics
author: Aristotle
openingChapterLabel: Chapter 1 — Imitation as the principle common to the arts
openingText: My subject is Poetry in itself and its various kinds. I will note the essential quality of each kind, and ask how the plot must be structured if a poem is to be good. I will also ask how many parts a poem has and what they are, and take up whatever else belongs to the same inquiry. I follow the order of nature, and so begin with the first principles.
about:
What makes a story hold together? Why are we moved by something we know is invented? In the Poetics, Aristotle examines poetry, especially tragedy and epic. He turns to Homer, Sophocles, Euripides, and other writers to understand how events, character, and language affect an audience.

Plot is central. Events do not make one story simply because they concern the same person. They must connect through probability or necessity. Aristotle also examines reversal, recognition, pity, and fear, and asks how poetry can express something universal while telling stories about invented people.

The text is brief and dense, and several works it mentions no longer survive. This edition modernizes S. H. Butcher's English translation, preserving its incomplete passages and marked textual supplements. Its discussion of language uses ancient categories for Greek, and Aristotle's judgments about women and enslaved people reflect his historical views.

angleCards.title: Why does plot come first?
angleCards.text: Aristotle calls plot the soul of tragedy. Examine why the connections between events matter more to him than the characters' qualities.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the argument for the priority of plot and test it against stories I know.

angleCards.title: What does imitation mean?
angleCards.text: Imitation includes images, music, dance, and poetry. Follow the links Aristotle makes between imitation, learning, and what could happen.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand mimesis and the difference between recording actual events and representing probable ones.

angleCards.title: When knowledge changes everything
angleCards.text: Recognition can reverse a situation. See why Aristotle prefers discoveries that grow from the action to recognitions brought about by arbitrary signs.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine recognition and reversal through the examples of Oedipus and Iphigenia.

angleCards.title: Why seek out tragedy?
angleCards.text: Pity and fear belong to tragedy's distinctive pleasure. Read the definition of catharsis alongside the examples of what moves an audience.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine what the text says about tragedy's emotional effects and what it leaves unresolved.

cast.name: Aristotle
cast.description: The philosopher studies poetry by distinguishing its forms and parts. He offers rules and reasons, considers examples, and answers objections. Readers can test his judgments rather than treating them as a checklist for every story.

cast.name: Oedipus
cast.description: Sophocles' tragedy shows how recognition can coincide with reversal. Aristotle returns to it repeatedly, while drawing examples from many other works. His account of tragedy does not rest on this play alone.

cast.name: Homer
cast.description: The Iliad and Odyssey help Aristotle examine unity, the narrator's role, and the wonderful. He praises Homer for selecting a limited action rather than telling everything about a war or a hero.

cast.name: Mimesis
cast.description: This concept links the arts Aristotle examines. They use different means to represent different things in different ways. Poetic imitation can show what might probably happen rather than simply copying an actual event.

cast.name: Catharsis
cast.description: Aristotle's definition of tragedy speaks of a purgation of pity and fear. This brief phrase does not receive an unambiguous explanation in the surviving text. Distinguish the wording itself from the interpretations readers may give it.

cast.name: Anagnorisis
cast.description: A change from ignorance to knowledge. It can reveal a person's identity and transform relationships. Aristotle prefers recognition that grows from the connected events, especially when it also reverses the situation.

whyItMatters.title: A vocabulary for stories
whyItMatters.body: Plot, character, reversal, and recognition give you precise questions to ask of a story. What brings about the next event? What would change if a scene disappeared? Aristotle makes these questions part of a sustained inquiry.

whyItMatters.title: Art and knowledge
whyItMatters.body: Aristotle calls poetry more philosophical than history because it aims at the universal. His claim invites us to ask how invented stories can teach us about human action without being factual reports.

whyItMatters.title: Rules worth questioning
whyItMatters.body: Aristotle prefers some kinds of endings and characters to others. That gives readers something to challenge: take a story that moves you and ask whether his account explains its effect or reveals the limits of his theory.
